idiom_name: modules as pluggable behaviour (include/extend); Forwardable for explicit delegation
implementation_notes: In Ruby a module is the reusable unit of behaviour: include puts its methods on every instance of a class, extend puts them on one object (the singleton class), and Module#ancestors shows the resulting composition - so the pattern's pluggable parts are usually modules plus ordinary collaborator objects in ivars rather than a component class hierarchy. obj.extend(Flyable) is the closest thing Ruby has to attaching a capability to a single instance at runtime. When the container should expose a component's methods as its own, Forwardable documents def_delegator/def_delegators explicitly as 'an alternative to inheritance' and DelegateClass handles whole-object delegation; there is no mainstream Ruby ECS, so the idiom replaces the structure rather than reproducing it.
code_sketch:
module Component
  def update(dt) = parts.each { |p| p.update(dt) }
end

class Actor
  include Component
  extend Forwardable
  def initialize(*parts)
    @parts = parts
  end
  def_delegators :@parts, :size, :each
end

bjorn = Actor.new(Input.new, Physics.new, Graphics.new)
bjorn.extend(Flyable)          # capability attached to this one instance
pitfalls: extend mixes behaviour into a single object's singleton class, so the capability is invisible in the object's class and cannot be discovered by code that inspects types - prefer a collaborator object when other code must see it.

Method-name collisions resolve by ancestor order: a module method silently overrides (or is overridden by) the object's own methods, so two components defining the same method cannot coexist without namespacing.
Forwardable's delegated methods are invisible to RDoc and to respond_to? unless the delegate responds, so public API surfaces should use explicit delegate objects instead.
